# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 6, 2026
**Re:** Breimourt Pictures Releasing LLC / Padisk Digital Cinema Services: Client Exposure Under the Supply Package
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Bottom Line

Breimourt is carrying more risk under the Padisk package than the deal as announced suggests. In order of significance to the client, the five problems are:

1. **The minimum commitment counts the wrong spend.** The Order Form's narrow "Covered Services" definition controls the US$850,000 Minimum Annual Commitment. Only physical drive duplication and shipment fees count toward it. Mastering, KDM and electronic delivery fees do not. Shortfall payments will therefore be inflated every year, and the gap widens as Breimourt moves to electronic delivery.
2. **The Contract Year 2 reduction notice was late.** The window closed January 15, 2026, and Breimourt's notice went out February 2, 2026. On the documents, Breimourt's position is weak. Contract Year 2 ends February 28, 2027, and Padisk will invoice any shortfall by around March 30, 2027.
3. **The exclusivity is far broader than the deal.** It is worldwide, it covers all media, and it binds Affiliates. The Order Form's US/Canada Territory does not narrow it. Breimourt may already be in breach if it or an Affiliate uses other vendors for streaming, airline, home-entertainment or foreign deliverables.
4. **Automatic three-year renewal.** Non-renewal notice must be *received* by **September 2, 2027**. If the date is missed, the minimums, the exclusivity and a 7% rate increase continue to February 2031.
5. **Split governing law and forum for the guaranty.** The Parent Guaranty is under Ontario law with an exclusive Toronto forum. The Supply Agreement is under New York law with an exclusive New York County forum. Breimourt could have to litigate twice, and the guarantor could relitigate the underlying obligations.

Most of these can be fixed or reduced through a single negotiated amendment. Breimourt has some leverage because Padisk wants the relationship to continue past 2028. Section 7 sets out a suggested package.

---

## 2. Key Commercial Terms (for reference)

| Term | Position | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Order Form Effective Date | March 1, 2025 | Order Form header; §2.1 |
| Initial Term | 3 years from March 1, 2025, ending **February 29, 2028** | Order Form §2.1 |
| Contract Years | 12-month periods from March 1 (CY1: Mar 1, 2025–Feb 28, 2026; CY2: Mar 1, 2026–Feb 28, 2027; CY3: Mar 1, 2027–Feb 29, 2028) | Supply Agreement §1.3; Order Form §2.2 |
| Minimum Annual Commitment | **US$850,000 in Covered Services fees per Contract Year**, including Renewal Terms; shortfall payable in full | Order Form §§3.1–3.2; Supply Agreement §5.2 |
| Renewal | Automatic, successive 3-year Renewal Terms unless 180 days' notice | Supply Agreement §2.2 |
| Rate escalator | +7% on all rates at the start of each Renewal Term | Order Form §4.3; Side Letter §2.3 |
| Territory | United States and Canada | Order Form §1.2 |
| Precedence | Supply Agreement prevails, except the Order Form controls pricing, the Initial Term and the Minimum Annual Commitment | Supply Agreement §14.3 |
| Governing law / forum (supply) | New York law; exclusive jurisdiction of state and federal courts in New York County | Supply Agreement §§15.1–15.2 |
| Governing law / forum (guaranty) | Ontario law; exclusive jurisdiction of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Toronto | Parent Guaranty §12 |
| Termination for convenience | None | Supply Agreement §13 |
| Liability cap | Does not apply to Customer's fees or shortfall payments | Supply Agreement §11.3(d) |

---

## 3. Ranked Issues

### Issue 1: "Covered Services" is redefined narrowly for the minimum commitment, so most of Breimourt's spend does not count

**Where it appears**
- Order Form §1.1: "As used in this Order Form, Covered Services means **physical DCP duplication and hard-drive shipment only**."
- Supply Agreement §1.4: the broad definition, covering DCP mastering, KDM generation, hard-drive duplication and shipment, and electronic delivery to exhibitors.
- Order Form §§3.1–3.3: the US$850,000 Minimum Annual Commitment is measured in "Covered Services fees," and any shortfall is payable "in full."
- Supply Agreement §14.3: the Order Form controls "the Minimum Annual Commitment."
- Side Letter §§2.3 and 4.1: electronic delivery is priced separately and nothing else is amended. The Side Letter does not bring electronic delivery fees into the minimum.
- Order Form §1.3: describes the ordered services as including mastering and KDM. This is inconsistent with §1.1 in the same document.

**Why it matters for Breimourt**
- Padisk will argue that §14.3 makes the Order Form control the minimum-commitment mechanics, including what counts toward the minimum. On that reading, only drive duplication and shipment fees count. Mastering (US$2,400–3,600 per feature version), KDMs (US$6.50 each) and all electronic delivery fees (US$62–74 per title per location from March 1, 2026) are excluded.
- The exposure grows over time. Each booking Breimourt moves from hard drive to electronic delivery reduces counting spend and increases the shortfall. Breimourt would pay Padisk for electronic delivery and then pay a second time as shortfall.
- For scale: a feature drive plus standard shipment is about US$133 per location. Reaching US$850,000 on counting spend alone would take roughly 6,400 drive-locations a year. That may well be unrealistic for an independent distributor's slate. We need actual volume data to confirm (see Section 4).
- The shortfall is uncapped (Supply Agreement §11.3(d)), and the issue repeats in every Contract Year, including Renewal Terms.

**Arguments available to Breimourt (moderate at best)**
- §14.3 gives the Order Form control over "the Minimum Annual Commitment." Breimourt can argue that this reaches the commitment amount and mechanics, but not a redefinition of a defined Supply Agreement term. On that view the Supply Agreement's §1.4 definition prevails on the conflict.
- Order Form §1.3, Supply Agreement §§3.1 and 5.1, and the overall structure all treat mastering, KDM and electronic delivery as Covered Services. Breimourt can argue that §1.1 should be read narrowly or treated as a drafting error.
- These are litigation arguments. The plain wording of §1.1 and the §14.3 carve-out favor Padisk.

**Recommended fix**
- Amend Order Form §1.1 to delete the narrow definition, or to conform it expressly to Supply Agreement §1.4. Confirm in writing that all fees for services ordered under the Order Form, including electronic delivery under the Side Letter, count toward the Minimum Annual Commitment.
- Make the amendment retroactive to CY1 and CY2.
- Fallback: reduce the US$850,000 figure so that it reflects realistic physical-delivery volume only.
- In the meantime, do not pay any shortfall invoice without a written reservation of rights. Review the CY1 annual statement under Order Form §3.5, and consider exercising audit rights under Supply Agreement §5.8.

---

### Issue 2: The Contract Year 2 reduction option expired before Breimourt's notice

**Where it appears**
- Order Form §3.4: a one-time option to reduce the CY2 minimum by up to 25%. Notice must be delivered "no later than **45 days before the first day of the second Contract Year**," in accordance with Supply Agreement §16.1.
- Supply Agreement §1.3 and Order Form §§2.1–2.2: the second Contract Year began **March 1, 2026**.
- Side Letter §§3.1–3.5: Breimourt delivered its Reduction Notice on **February 2, 2026**, electing US$637,500. Padisk rejected it as untimely by letter of February 9, 2026. Breimourt disputes the rejection. Both parties reserve all rights, and disputes go to Supply Agreement §15.

**Why it matters for Breimourt**
- The deadline was **January 15, 2026**: 45 days before March 1, 2026, counting the 28 days of February and 17 days of January. Breimourt's **February 2, 2026 notice was late**, by 18 days. On the documents as drafted, Breimourt's position is weak.
- The amount at stake is US$212,500 of minimum-commitment reduction (US$850,000 vs. US$637,500) for CY2. Combined with Issue 1, the actual CY2 shortfall could be much larger than that.
- Timing: CY2 ends February 28, 2027. Padisk must invoice the Shortfall Amount within 30 days after year-end (Order Form §3.2), and payment is due 30 days after receipt (Supply Agreement §5.4). Late amounts bear interest at up to 1% per month (§5.6).
- The Side Letter's reservation of rights (§3.4) keeps the dispute open but does not improve Breimourt's position. Supply Agreement §16.8 requires any waiver by Padisk to be in writing and signed.

**Recommended fix**
- Do not tell the client the notice was timely. Advise that the position is weak, but keep the reservation of rights in place and avoid any written concession.
- Check whether any facts support waiver or estoppel. For example, did Padisk represent a different deadline, accept late elections in other contexts, or act on the reduced figure? Also confirm that the notice was delivered by a method permitted under §16.1.
- Seek a negotiated outcome before the CY2 shortfall is invoiced. Options include a signed amendment under Supply Agreement §14.2 accepting the reduction (or a partial reduction), a credit, or a reduction folded into the Issue 1 fix.
- If the matter is not resolved, invoke the §15.3 executive escalation before any proceeding. Treat any withholding under §5.5 with caution, because it must be a good-faith dispute.
- Going forward, calendar every contractual notice date with an internal deadline at least 30 days early.

---

### Issue 3: The exclusivity is worldwide, covers all media, and binds Affiliates

**Where it appears**
- Supply Agreement §4.1: Customer "shall, and shall cause its Affiliates to, obtain all of their requirements for Exclusive Services **throughout the world** solely from Supplier."
- Supply Agreement §4.2: no third-party providers and no self-performance by Customer or any Affiliate.
- Supply Agreement §1.7: "Exclusive Services" means mastering, encoding and delivery services for any Content.
- Supply Agreement §1.5: "Content" means any audiovisual work "**in any medium**, including theatrical, streaming, airline, and home-entertainment deliverables," distributed by Customer or any Affiliate.
- Supply Agreement §1.1: "Affiliate" includes any entity that controls Breimourt, is controlled by it, or is under common control with it.
- Order Form §§1.2–1.3: Territory is the United States and Canada, and the ordered scope is theatrical DCP services for Breimourt's theatrical releases.
- Supply Agreement §14.3: the Order Form controls only pricing, the Initial Term and the Minimum Annual Commitment.

**Why it matters for Breimourt**
- Under §14.3 the Supply Agreement prevails on all other conflicts, including exclusivity. **The Order Form's US/Canada Territory therefore does not narrow the exclusivity.** On its terms, the obligation reaches the following:
  - Breimourt's non-theatrical deliverables, such as streaming, airline and home-entertainment masters and encodes;
  - foreign deliverables; and
  - any parent, sister or subsidiary company, including entities Breimourt does not control. Breimourt cannot "cause" a parent or sister company to comply, yet it is still liable if they do not.
- Breimourt and its Affiliates may already be in breach if they use other post-production or delivery vendors. That creates exposure to a for-cause termination under §13.1 and to damages claims. It also gives Padisk leverage in the Issue 1 and Issue 2 disputes.
- The exclusivity runs for the whole Term, including Renewal Terms (§§1.14, 4.1). It will also constrain any future acquisition or affiliation transaction.
- The March 4, 2025 press release describes the deal as US/Canada theatrical delivery. It has no contractual effect, but it helps in negotiation to show that the drafting goes beyond the commercial intent.

**Recommended fix**
- Amend §§1.5, 1.7, 4.1 and 4.2 so that the exclusivity covers only theatrical Covered Services for Breimourt's own theatrical releases in the Territory. Remove Affiliates entirely, or limit them to controlled subsidiaries that adopt the arrangement by election.
- Add an express carve-out for non-theatrical, foreign and Affiliate deliverables, and preserve Breimourt's right to use third parties where Padisk cannot meet a delivery date.
- Immediately, confirm with the client which vendors Breimourt and its Affiliates currently use for any mastering, encoding or delivery work, so that we can assess any existing breach before we raise the point with Padisk.

---

### Issue 4: Automatic three-year renewal, with a non-renewal deadline of September 2, 2027

**Where it appears**
- Supply Agreement §2.2: automatic renewal "for successive Renewal Terms of three (3) years each" unless written notice of non-renewal is given "at least one hundred eighty (180) days before expiry of the then-current term." Each Renewal Term runs on the Agreement and Order Form "then in effect."
- Order Form §2.1: the Initial Term ends February 29, 2028.
- Order Form §3.1: the Minimum Annual Commitment applies in every Contract Year of any Renewal Term.
- Order Form §4.3 and Side Letter §2.3: all rates, including electronic delivery rates, increase 7% at the start of each Renewal Term.
- Supply Agreement §4.1: the exclusivity runs for the whole Term.
- Supply Agreement §16.1: notice is effective only on receipt, and must be delivered by hand, by overnight courier, or by email with a courier confirmation copy.

**Why it matters for Breimourt**
- Measured 180 days back from the February 29, 2028 expiry, the last day for non-renewal notice is **September 2, 2027**. Notice must be *received* by then.
- Missing the date by one day locks Breimourt in until February 2031. It would face three more years of the US$850,000 minimum (with the Issue 1 problem still in place unless fixed), the worldwide exclusivity, and 7% higher rates. There is no termination for convenience, and the shortfall is uncapped.
- The clause binds both parties alike, but in practice the burden falls on Breimourt as the committed buyer.

**Recommended fix**
- Calendar now. Set an internal decision date of about June 1, 2027 and a target delivery date for any notice of no later than August 1, 2027, to avoid disputes over day-counting or receipt. Use both courier and email under §16.1.
- In the amendment, seek either of the following:
  - renewal only by mutual written agreement; or
  - one-year renewal terms with a shorter notice period, such as 60–90 days.
- Also seek removal or capping of the 7% escalator (for example, CPI-linked), a step-down or removal of the minimum in any Renewal Term, and a termination-for-convenience right on notice.
- Consider whether a protective non-renewal notice should be served in mid-2027 to preserve leverage, with renewal then negotiated on new terms.

---

### Issue 5: The Parent Guaranty is under Ontario law with an exclusive Toronto forum, which conflicts with the New York-law Supply Agreement

**Where it appears**
- Parent Guaranty §12.1: Ontario law and applicable Canadian federal law govern the Guaranty "and any claim or dispute arising out of or relating to this Guaranty **or the Guaranteed Obligations**."
- Parent Guaranty §12.2: exclusive jurisdiction of the **Ontario Superior Court of Justice** sitting in Toronto.
- Supply Agreement §§15.1–15.2: New York law and exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County.
- Parent Guaranty §2.1: the guaranty covers only service credits and refunds (§6.5), refunds and credits on termination (§13.3(b)), indemnities (§10.1), and enforcement costs.
- Supply Agreement §14.3: the precedence clause does not address the Guaranty, and the guarantor is not a party to the Supply Agreement's forum clause.

**Why it matters for Breimourt**
- To enforce against Padisk and its parent, Breimourt would sue Padisk in New York under New York law and then sue Padisk Holdings in Toronto under Ontario law. That means two sets of counsel, added cost and delay, and a risk of inconsistent results.
- Because §12 extends to disputes relating to "the Guaranteed Obligations," the guarantor can argue that whether and how much Padisk owes must itself be decided in Toronto. It could then relitigate liability even after a New York judgment.
- The Guaranty is a guaranty of payment and a primary obligation (§§2.3, 3.1). Those features help Breimourt, but the forum split undercuts them in practice.
- Related point: the Guaranty does not cover Padisk's performance generally, such as damages for breach or the warranty obligations under §9.2. It covers only the listed payment items. This is narrower than the matter summary's description of the Guaranty as covering "performance obligations," and the client should understand that limit.

**Recommended fix**
- Amend Parent Guaranty §12 to adopt New York law and the New York County forum, matching Supply Agreement §15.
- Add the following:
  - a submission to jurisdiction by the guarantor;
  - appointment of a New York agent for service of process; and
  - an agreement that any judgment, award or settlement binding Padisk is conclusive against the guarantor as to the existence and amount of the Guaranteed Obligations.
- If Padisk Holdings will not move off Ontario law, the minimum fallback is non-exclusive Ontario jurisdiction plus the conclusive-judgment undertaking.
- Consider broadening §2.1 to cover all of Padisk's payment and performance obligations under the Agreement, including damages for breach.

---

## 4. Gaps and Points Needing Confirmation

These items limit the analysis. I have not filled them with assumptions.

1. **Execution status.** All signature blocks in the copies provided are blank, including the Side Letter countersignature. We need fully executed versions of each document, and confirmation that there are no other amendments or side letters.
2. **Spend and volume data.** I have no invoices, no CY1 annual statement under Order Form §3.5, and no Release Schedules. Without them I cannot quantify CY1 or likely CY2 shortfall under either reading of "Covered Services." Was a CY1 shortfall invoiced or paid, and on what basis? Payment without objection could be cited by Padisk as course of dealing.
3. **The notices themselves.** The February 2, 2026 Reduction Notice and Padisk's February 9, 2026 rejection letter are not in the folder. We need them, together with any earlier correspondence, to check delivery method under §16.1 and to look for any waiver or estoppel facts.
4. **Interim electronic delivery rates.** Side Letter §2.2 confirms pre-March 2026 electronic delivery invoices "as final" at interim rates we have not seen. We should confirm the client was comfortable with those rates before signing.
5. **Affiliates and other vendors.** We need Breimourt's corporate structure and a list of current non-Padisk vendors for any mastering, encoding or delivery work, in any medium and anywhere in the world, to assess the Issue 3 breach exposure.
6. **Initial Term end date.** "3 years from March 1, 2025" could be read as ending at midnight on February 29, 2028 or on March 1, 2028. This is why the recommended notice date is well ahead of September 2, 2027.
7. **Press release.** This is a marketing document with no contractual effect, and I have not relied on it for any term. It is useful only as evidence of the commercial intent (US/Canada, theatrical) in negotiations.

---

## 5. Suggested Talking Points for the Client Call

- "The biggest money risk is that most of what you pay Padisk does not count toward the $850,000 minimum. We want that fixed retroactively."
- "Your February notice to reduce Year 2 was 18 days late. We are preserving your position, but the realistic route is a negotiated deal before the Year 2 shortfall bill arrives around March 2027."
- "On paper, the exclusivity covers everything you or any related company deliver, in any medium, anywhere. We need to know today what other vendors you use."
- "Put September 2, 2027 in every calendar. Miss it and you are locked in until 2031 at 7% higher rates. Our recommendation is to decide by June 2027 and send any notice by August 1, 2027."
- "The parent guarantee only covers credits, refunds and indemnities, and it has to be enforced in Toronto under Ontario law. We want it moved to New York."

---

## 6. Recommended Next Steps

1. Obtain the missing documents and data listed in Section 4, ideally within two weeks.
2. Run a privileged internal check of Affiliate and third-party vendor use (Issue 3).
3. Model the CY1 and CY2 shortfall under both readings of "Covered Services," with and without the 25% reduction.
4. Prepare a single amendment package covering Issues 1–5 and approach Padisk before the CY2 year-end (February 28, 2027).
5. Docket: CY2 year-end on February 28, 2027; shortfall invoice expected by about March 30, 2027; internal renewal decision by June 1, 2027; non-renewal notice target of August 1, 2027; hard deadline of **September 2, 2027**.

---

## 7. Proposed Negotiation Package (single amendment under Supply Agreement §14.2)

| # | Ask | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Conform Order Form §1.1 to Supply Agreement §1.4, retroactive to CY1 | Lower the minimum to reflect physical-only counting |
| 2 | Accept the CY2 reduction to US$637,500 | Partial reduction or credit |
| 3 | Limit exclusivity to theatrical Covered Services, Breimourt's own releases, in the Territory; remove Affiliates | Limit Affiliates to controlled subsidiaries; add express non-theatrical and foreign carve-out |
| 4 | Renewal only by mutual agreement; remove the 7% escalator | One-year renewals with 60–90 days' notice; CPI cap |
| 5 | Move the Guaranty to New York law and forum; add a conclusive-judgment clause; broaden its scope | Non-exclusive Ontario forum plus the conclusive-judgment undertaking |

Breimourt's leverage comes from Padisk's interest in renewal beyond 2028 and from the value of a clean, expandable relationship (for example, adding non-theatrical work by choice rather than by compulsion). Breimourt's main weaknesses are Issue 2 and any existing breach under Issue 3, so we should establish the facts on Issue 3 before we open discussions.

**Re:** Breimourt Pictures Releasing LLC: exposure under the Padisk digital cinema services documents

**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed the five documents in the folder:

- **Supply Agreement** (supply_agreement.md, dated March 1, 2025). New York law; exclusive forum in the New York County courts.
- **Order Form** No. BPR-PDCS-001 (order_form.md, Order Form Effective Date March 1, 2025).
- **Parent Guaranty** by Padisk Holdings Ltd. (parent_guaranty.md, dated March 1, 2025).
- **Side Letter** on electronic delivery rates and the reduction notice (side_letter_electronic_delivery.md, dated February 20, 2026).
- **Press Release** dated March 4, 2025 (press_release.md).

The press release is marketing material only. Its description of a "United States and Canada" theatrical deal does not change the contract terms. Breimourt should not rely on it as evidence of a narrower deal.

**Key commercial terms:**

- **Initial Term.** Three years from March 1, 2025, ending February 29, 2028 (Order Form §2.1).
- **Minimum Annual Commitment.** US$850,000 in "Covered Services" fees per Contract Year (Order Form §3.1).

The four issues below are ranked by significance to the client. The two minimum-commitment issues come first because they are near-term cash exposure. The Contract Year 2 shortfall will be invoiced within 30 days after February 28, 2027.

---

## 2. Issues (ranked)

### Issue 1: "Covered Services" is redefined narrowly in the Order Form, so most of Breimourt's spend does not count toward the US$850,000 minimum

**Where it appears**

- Order Form §1.1: "As used in this Order Form, Covered Services means physical DCP duplication and hard-drive shipment only."
- Supply Agreement §1.4: the broader definition, covering DCP mastering, KDM generation, hard-drive duplication and shipment, and electronic delivery to exhibitors.
- Order Form §3.1 (Minimum Annual Commitment measured in "Covered Services fees"), §3.2 (shortfall payable in full) and §3.3 (calculation).
- Supply Agreement §14.3 (precedence) and §5.2.
- Side Letter §§2.1–2.3 and §4.1 (electronic delivery is priced separately, and "nothing in this Side Letter amends" anything else).

**Why it matters**

- The minimum is measured in "Covered Services fees" under the Order Form, and the Order Form defines that term narrowly.
- Supply Agreement §14.3 gives the Order Form control over the Minimum Annual Commitment. Padisk will argue that the narrow definition therefore governs the calculation.
- On that reading, only physical drive duplication and shipment fees count. Mastering (US$2,400–3,600 per feature version), KDMs, QC and all electronic delivery fees would be excluded. Electronic delivery is now priced at US$62 or US$74 per title, per location under the Side Letter.
- As the industry moves from hard drives to electronic delivery, Breimourt's countable spend shrinks while its total spend with Padisk may stay the same or grow.
- The practical result is that Breimourt could pay Padisk well over US$850,000 in a year and still owe a large shortfall payment.
- The Side Letter does not help. It prices electronic delivery but expressly makes no other amendment (§4.1), so it does not bring that spend within the minimum.
- Breimourt has a counter-argument. Supply Agreement §14.3 gives the Order Form control over the *Minimum Annual Commitment*, not over definitions. The Supply Agreement definition would then prevail as a conflicting term. The point is genuinely contestable, but the Order Form language is express and specific, so Breimourt should not count on winning it.

**Recommended fix**

- Seek a written amendment under Supply Agreement §14.2 that deletes Order Form §1.1 or conforms it to Supply Agreement §1.4.
- The amendment should state expressly that mastering, KDM, QC and electronic delivery fees count toward the Minimum Annual Commitment.
- Ask the client for its Contract Year 1 annual statement (Order Form §3.5). We need to know whether Padisk has already calculated and invoiced a Contract Year 1 shortfall on the narrow basis, and whether Breimourt paid it.
- If Breimourt did pay on that basis, consider an audit under Supply Agreement §5.8 and a reservation of rights.

---

### Issue 2: The Contract Year 2 reduction option expired before Breimourt's notice, so Breimourt faces the full minimum for Contract Year 2

**Where it appears**

- Order Form §3.4: a one-time option to reduce the Contract Year 2 minimum by up to 25%, exercisable by notice "no later than 45 days before the first day of the second Contract Year."
- Supply Agreement §1.3 and Order Form §§2.1–2.2: Contract Year 2 begins March 1, 2026.
- Side Letter §§3.1–3.5: records the February 2, 2026 Reduction Notice (reducing the minimum to US$637,500), Padisk's February 9, 2026 rejection as untimely, Breimourt's dispute, a mutual reservation of rights, and dispute resolution under Supply Agreement §15.
- Supply Agreement §16.1: notice formalities. The notice is effective on receipt.

**Why it matters**

- Forty-five days before March 1, 2026 is **January 15, 2026**.
- **Breimourt's February 2, 2026 notice was late** by about 18 days.
- On the documents as they stand, Padisk's rejection is well-founded. Breimourt's recorded position that the notice is effective is weak.
- Unless the parties agree otherwise, the Contract Year 2 minimum remains US$850,000, not US$637,500.
- That is up to US$212,500 of additional potential shortfall exposure. It compounds Issue 1, because only the narrowly defined "Covered Services" fees count toward that US$850,000.
- Supply Agreement §16.8 requires waivers to be in writing and signed. Breimourt therefore cannot easily argue informal waiver unless there is written correspondence we have not seen.

**Recommended fix**

- Maintain the reservation of rights in Side Letter §3.4. Do not take any step that could be read as conceding the point.
- Ask the client whether any earlier written communication could arguably constitute notice before January 15, 2026. Examples are a Release Schedule, emails to the account representative, or budget discussions. Also ask whether Padisk said anything that might support an estoppel argument.
- Commercially, seek a negotiated amendment before the Contract Year 2 shortfall is invoiced in March 2027. This could be a full or partial reduction, a carry-forward of excess spend, or resolution of the reduction alongside Issue 1.
- Budget for full Contract Year 2 exposure in the meantime.
- Follow the escalation step in Supply Agreement §15.3 before any proceeding.

---

### Issue 3: The exclusivity is worldwide, covers all media and binds Breimourt's Affiliates, and the Order Form's Territory does not narrow it

**Where it appears**

- Supply Agreement §4.1: Customer "shall, and shall cause its Affiliates to, obtain all of their requirements for Exclusive Services **throughout the world** solely from Supplier."
- Supply Agreement §4.2: no third-party providers and no self-supply.
- Supply Agreement §1.7: "Exclusive Services" means mastering, encoding and delivery services for any Content.
- Supply Agreement §1.5: "Content" means any audiovisual work "**in any medium**, including theatrical, streaming, airline, and home-entertainment deliverables," distributed by Customer or its Affiliates.
- Supply Agreement §1.1: definition of "Affiliate."
- Order Form §1.2 (Territory: United States and Canada) and §1.3 (theatrical DCP services for theatrical releases in the Territory).
- Supply Agreement §14.3 (precedence).

**Why it matters**

- The commercial deal, as reflected in the Order Form and the press release, is theatrical delivery in the United States and Canada. The exclusivity is far broader.
- Under §14.3, the Order Form controls only pricing, the Initial Term and the Minimum Annual Commitment. On every other conflict the Supply Agreement prevails. **The Order Form's United States and Canada Territory therefore does not limit the exclusivity.**
- As drafted, Breimourt and every Affiliate must use Padisk worldwide for all mastering, encoding and delivery of any audiovisual work. That reaches streaming, airline and home-entertainment deliverables, foreign releases, and in-house encoding work.
- Breimourt is in breach today if any Affiliate, or Breimourt itself, uses another vendor or does such work internally. That exposes it to a §13.1 termination-for-cause claim and damages.
- The clause also constrains any future acquirer or group restructuring. "Affiliate" includes parents and sister companies under common control.
- Padisk's contractual obligations are not correspondingly broad. It is committed to capacity only for the theatrical Release Schedule (§4.3), and it may not even offer some of these services.

**Recommended fix**

- Amend Supply Agreement §§4.1–4.2, and §1.7 as needed, to limit exclusivity to theatrical DCP services for Breimourt's own theatrical releases in the Territory.
- Delete the Affiliate obligation.
- Expressly carve out non-theatrical media, territories outside the United States and Canada, and in-house work.
- Add a right to use third parties where Padisk cannot meet a requirement. At present this right exists only under force majeure (§16.4).
- Ask the client now to confirm whether Breimourt or any Affiliate currently uses other vendors or does in-house encoding or delivery. We need to assess existing breach exposure before raising the point with Padisk.

### Issue 4: The Parent Guaranty is governed by Ontario law with an exclusive Toronto forum, which conflicts with the New York law and forum in the Supply Agreement

**Where it appears**

- Parent Guaranty §12.1: Ontario law and applicable Canadian federal law.
- Parent Guaranty §12.2: exclusive jurisdiction of the **Ontario Superior Court of Justice** in Toronto for disputes "arising out of or relating to this Guaranty or the Guaranteed Obligations."
- Supply Agreement §15.1 (New York law) and §15.2 (exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County).
- Parent Guaranty §2.1 (scope of Guaranteed Obligations) and §3.1 (primary obligation; separate action).

**Why it matters**

- If Padisk defaults, Breimourt must sue Padisk in New York under New York law. It must then pursue Padisk Holdings in Toronto under Ontario law.
- The Toronto clause expressly covers disputes relating to "the Guaranteed Obligations." The guarantor can therefore argue that the Ontario court must decide afresh whether, and how much, Padisk owes. A New York judgment against Padisk may not bind it.
- The result is two proceedings, duplicated cost and delay, and a risk of inconsistent outcomes. That undermines the value of the guaranty precisely when Breimourt needs it, typically on Padisk's insolvency.
- The guaranty is also narrow in substance. It covers only service credits and refunds (§§6.5, 13.3(b)), Supplier indemnities (§10.1) and enforcement costs. It does not guarantee Padisk's performance generally, damages for breach, or the cost of replacement services.
- The guaranty is not listed in the Supply Agreement precedence clause (§14.3). Nothing in the Supply Agreement binds the guarantor to the New York forum.

**Recommended fix**

- Amend Parent Guaranty §12 to adopt New York law and the New York County forum, consistent with Supply Agreement §§15.1–15.2.
- Add a guarantor agreement to be bound by any judgment or settlement against Padisk on the underlying obligations.
- Require Padisk Holdings to appoint an agent for service of process in New York.
- If Padisk resists, at minimum seek non-exclusive jurisdiction so that Breimourt can join the guarantor in the New York action.
- Consider asking for the scope of §2.1 to be expanded to cover Padisk's damages for breach and re-performance costs.
